description:
Russia's Vostok Station, deep inland on the Antarctic ice sheet, recorded -89.2 degrees Celsius on 21 July 1983, the lowest natural temperature ever confirmed on Earth's surface. This is the coldest figure measured directly. Satellite readings have since detected colder spots elsewhere on the ice sheet.

the coldest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth's surface, recorded at Vostok Station on 21 July 1983.

Even Vostok's warmest moment on record was brutally cold: -14 degrees Celsius, once, in the middle of the Southern Hemisphere summer. That single reading, on 5 January 1974, is still the warmest this station has ever recorded.

In December it receives an average of about 709 hours of sunshine, nearly 23 hours a day, more than the sunniest spots near the Sahara. It gets zero sunshine at all for roughly four months of the year, May to August, so the sunniest claim is about total hours across the year, not constant daylight.

Beneath all that ice sits Lake Vostok, a liquid freshwater lake sealed under about four kilometres of ice for millions of years. Scientists did not physically reach its surface with a drill until 5 February 2012.
